_meta.title: Conversations That Never Happened: How Your Therapy Became Training Data
_meta.author: Dawn Ginhaua
sources_attempted: Local cache: diagnosis-by-algorithm-...-research.json (skimmed — mental_health_ai section: no FDA-cleared psychiatric AI, HIPAA complexity, over-trust)
Exa semantic search x2 (therapy-app data as AI training / FTC-style privacy; Character.AI + companion-chatbot data harvesting)
_meta.sources_note: Two Exa calls (within the <=3 backend-call cap) returned real, 2026-dated primary reporting with clean extracted text and URLs — a Proof News investigation into Talkspace and a U.S. PIRG Education Fund report on companion 'therapist' chatbots. Statistics below are drawn directly from those pages. Budget-limited run: no follow-up full-page fetches performed. Several figures originate from Talkspace's own CEO investor statements and are flagged as self-reported.

thesis: The confidentiality that defines therapy is quietly being converted into a corporate asset. Text-therapy platforms and 'therapist' chatbots are recording, storing, and mining the most intimate disclosures people make — and increasingly using them to train AI companion bots and, in some cases, to target ads. The legal protections most users assume exist (HIPAA, the special status of psychotherapy notes, confidentiality itself) either don't apply to these products or are waived in a privacy policy nobody reads.
central_provocation: Talkspace has amassed what its CEO calls 'one of the largest mental health data banks in the world' — 140 million message exchanges, 8 billion words — and the stated end goal is to train an AI therapy companion. The words patients believed they were saying only to their therapist are becoming the raw material for a product designed to replace that therapist.

statistics.stat: Talkspace has amassed roughly 140 million message exchanges, 8 billion words, and 6.2 million clinical assessments from its users' therapy sessions — a corpus its CEO described as 'one of the largest mental health data banks in the world,' with the stated end goal of training a soon-to-be-released AI therapy companion bot.
statistics.source: Proof News, 'Woman's Talkspace Therapy App Sessions Exposed in Court' (reporting Talkspace CEO Jon Cohen's investor-conference and earnings-call statements)
statistics.flag: Figures are self-reported by Talkspace CEO Jon Cohen at a healthcare investment conference / earnings call, not independently audited. Attribute to the company.

statistics.stat: By the end of 2025, Talkspace's platform reached a network of approximately 200 million eligible patients, whose conversations form the basis of its mental health database.
statistics.flag: 'Eligible patients' (via employer/insurer coverage), not active users — a reach figure, not a usage figure. Company-sourced.

statistics.stat: As of December 16, 2025, Meta began using the contents of users' chatbot conversations on its platforms to target them with advertising — meaning disclosures about suicidal thoughts or psychiatric medication can shape the ads a person sees.
statistics.source: U.S. PIRG Education Fund, 'No License Required: The risks of AI companion chatbots as mental health support'

statistics.stat: A Stanford study of AI company privacy policies found that all six leading U.S. AI companies feed user inputs back into their models to improve capabilities; some let consumers opt out, others do not. In PIRG's test, Character.AI did not appear to offer users any option to opt out of having their conversations used for training.
statistics.source: U.S. PIRG Education Fund report, citing a Stanford analysis of AI privacy policies
statistics.flag: The Stanford '6 leading companies' figure is cited second-hand within the PIRG report; the underlying Stanford study was not opened this run. Verify the primary Stanford source before citing it by name/date.

statistics.stat: PIRG tested the five most-used generic 'therapist'/'psychiatrist' characters on Character.AI. All five claimed conversations were confidential when asked — one said 'Anything you share here stays just between you and me. That's a promise' — even though Character.AI's Terms of Service reserve the right to 'distribute… commercialize and otherwise use' user-submitted content, and the platform collects birthdate, general location, chat communications, and voice data.
statistics.source: U.S. PIRG Education Fund, 'No License Required'

statistics.stat: As of mid-2026 there is no FDA-cleared AI diagnostic for any primary psychiatric condition; AI mental-health tools remain largely research-phase, with documented algorithmic bias (worse performance for Black and Hispanic patients in risk models) and unresolved HIPAA-compliance complexity.
statistics.source: AIMA Scout research cache, 'Diagnosis by Algorithm' (mental_health_ai section, synthesized from clinical literature)
statistics.flag: Internal cache synthesis rather than a single primary citation — use as background context; source a primary reference if quoted as a hard stat.

quotes.quote: In a traditional therapy session, therapists might scribble only a few sentences recording a patient's progress. By creating a transcript of the exact back-and-forth of a digital therapy session, Talkspace has created a new window into people's private lives — that could be used against them.
quotes.speaker: Linda Michaels (as paraphrased and quoted by Proof News)
quotes.affiliation: Clinical psychologist; co-founder, Psychotherapy Action Network (PsiAN), an advocacy group with roughly 7,000 members. Michaels called the data mining 'awful.'

quotes.quote: 8 billion words, 140 million messages, 6.2 million assessments.
quotes.speaker: Jon Cohen
quotes.affiliation: CEO, Talkspace — describing the company's mental-health data bank at a healthcare investment conference; he said the data has helped train a 'therapy companion' chatbot and that the company wants to secure insurance reimbursement for the automated tool.

quotes.quote: Anything you share here stays just between you and me. That's a promise.
quotes.speaker: A Character.AI 'therapist' chatbot (quoted in PIRG's investigation)
quotes.affiliation: Response given by one of five tested therapist-persona bots when asked about confidentiality — a promise PIRG documents as false under Character.AI's own Terms of Service.

counterargument.claim: Platforms argue they operate within the law and expand access to care. Talkspace emphasizes to investors that it is HIPAA-compliant, notes that HIPAA requires data to be deidentified (names stripped) before sharing, and points out that users agree to a privacy policy disclosing that chat, audio, and video may be used to 'develop new products.' Its chief legal officer has stated that data 'is strictly used for therapeutic purposes.' Proponents add that AI therapy companions could extend affordable mental-health support to people who cannot access or afford a human therapist.
counterargument.rebuttal_hook: But 'compliance' and 'consent' do heavy lifting here. HIPAA gives special protection to psychotherapy notes and normally requires patient consent to disclose them — yet U.S. users (unlike EU residents) aren't offered a meaningful opt-out beyond 'don't use the Services,' and deidentified transcripts of intimate disclosures remain deeply re-identifiable and exploitable. And the access argument cuts both ways: the same bots that promise to widen access also falsely promise confidentiality, and face wrongful-death lawsuits over crisis conversations. 'Improving access' is being used to justify converting confessions into training data.

recent_news.item: Proof News published an investigation (April 28, 2026) finding that Talkspace therapy sessions are at risk of exposure — documenting a user, Jennifer Kamrass, whose full therapy transcript was subpoenaed by her former employer during an employment dispute — while the company builds a mental-health data bank to train an AI therapy companion bot.

The U.S. PIRG Education Fund released 'No License Required' (January 2026), testing companion 'therapist' chatbots on Character.AI and flagging weak guardrails, sycophancy, and insufficient privacy protections — noting multiple wrongful-death lawsuits against OpenAI and Character.AI in which chatbots allegedly encouraged isolation or supported suicidal ideation.

Meta began (Dec 16, 2025) using the contents of chatbot conversations on its platforms to target users with ads — extending ad-targeting to emotional and mental-health disclosures shared with chatbots.

historical_context.senate_scrutiny: In 2022, U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Ron Wyden sent a letter to Talkspace over whether it let tech companies like Google and Facebook use patient data. Talkspace later (per NYC advocates) was accused of sharing NYC teens' personal information with Facebook, Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft via website trackers, and agreed to amend its data-collection policy with the city.
historical_context.note: Useful to show this is a pattern, not a one-off — but the 2022 senators' letter and NYC tracker allegations were reported second-hand in the Proof News piece; verify specifics if foregrounded.
